c1.story:
Think about the last song you heard today. Maybe it was an old Kishore Kumar number in a reel, a new Punjabi track on Spotify, or a film song blaring at a wedding sangeet. Somebody got paid for that play, and there is a fair chance it was a company listed on the NSE that bought the rights decades ago and has been collecting ever since.

Now think about the last time you watched a TV channel live. For many urban Indians, it has been a while. That contrast, between the old song that keeps paying and the TV channel that keeps shrinking, is the entire media sector in one picture.

The listed companies sit behind four doors. The first is broadcasters and streamers: Sun TV, Zee and Reliance's Network group. They earn from advertising and from subscription fees paid through cable, DTH and streaming apps. But their content wears out. A serial airs, gets watched and is gone, so they must buy or commission fresh content every single year just to stand still.

The second is music and film rights owners: Saregama, which inherited the old HMV catalogue of Hindi film music, Tips, and Panorama. They own a catalogue and license it to streaming apps, TV, short-video platforms and brands, year after year. The song was paid for once. It earns forever.

The third is theatres and experiences: PVR INOX's multiplexes and Imagicaa's amusement park. Tickets, popcorn, on-screen ads. A full house when the film is good; an empty one when it is not.

The fourth is print, outdoor and content services: DB Corp's Dainik Bhaskar, Signpost's billboards, Prime Focus doing visual effects for Hollywood, MPS doing publishing work. Mature cash flows, or a services order book.

A broadcaster pays for its content every year. A music label paid once, and the song keeps working.

That one difference is why the market pays far more per rupee of profit for music labels than for TV channels. Before you ask whether media is a good sector, ask which door.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, and compare the bars before anything else.

  • The name and the line under it describe how money comes in: advertising plus subscriptions with content bought every year; licensing a catalogue again and again; tickets, food and on-screen ads; or newspaper ads, billboards and contract services.
  • The tickers are listed names mostly behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Some companies straddle: a broadcaster may also own a film library, and a music label may produce films.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company keeps. Music and film rights owners sit at high: the content is paid for and every new licence is mostly profit. Broadcasters and theatres sit at medium. Print, outdoor and services sit at low.
  • The bet line is what you are wagering on: ad budgets and TV declining slower than feared; streaming royalties rising and the catalogue being played forever; the film slate and families leaving the house; cash flow from a mature business or a services order book.

Then read the analogy: the chai stall with a TV, the owner of the songs the stall plays, the mela tent, and the poster printer. The so-what underneath states the key rule: earning every time anyone plays your content beats paying again for new content every year, which is why the multiples differ so much between the first two tiles.

c2.story:
Every piece of content you consume passes through five stations, and the decade's biggest story is that the fourth station changed hands.

The first station is talent and ideas: writers, directors, actors, composers, and the cricket boards whose matches are the most valuable content in India. The BCCI is the single most powerful supplier in this kitchen.

The second is rights and catalogues. Somebody buys the rights to songs, films, shows and sports, for a few years or forever. Saregama, Tips, Panorama, Sun TV, Zee and the Reliance-Disney combine stand here. Owning rights is owning the toll on everything downstream.

The third is packaging and production: editing, dubbing, visual effects, scheduling into channels and apps. Prime Focus, whose DNEG studio has won Oscars for its visual effects work, and MPS, doing publishing services, stand here, along with broadcasters' in-house studios.

The fourth is distribution, and this is where everything shifted. Ten years ago, Indian cable operators, DTH companies and newspapers were the pipes. Today the pipes are YouTube, Instagram, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and JioHotstar, alongside cinema screens. Most of these are global platforms, and they also capture most of India's digital ad money.

The fifth is the audience and the advertiser: households paying subscriptions, cinema-goers buying tickets, and FMCG, auto, telecom and e-commerce brands paying for attention.

Distribution moved to Google, Meta and Netflix. Content ownership stayed home.

That is the most useful idea on this page. Whoever owns the content keeps pricing power even when distribution changes hands, because every new platform still needs songs and films. Whoever only distributes is squeezed. A music label sells to YouTube; a TV channel competes with it. Geography adds texture: Mumbai for Hindi film, TV and music, Chennai and Hyderabad for southern-language content, which now travels nationally, as a string of Telugu and Kannada blockbusters has proved.
c2.read:
Two layers: five stations across the top, and a band row underneath showing who holds each.

The five boxes run from talent and ideas on the left to audience and advertiser on the right. Under each, read what happens and who stands there. The cast changes as you move right: producers, composers and the BCCI; rights owners including the listed labels and broadcasters; visual-effects and publishing services; DTH, cable, multiplexes and global platforms; households and advertisers.

The band row is the summary. The first cell is creators. The two coloured India listed cells sit under rights and catalogues, and under packaging and production. The distribution cell is marked global platforms and coloured as the rival. The last cell is viewers and advertisers.

Read the picture this way: Indian listed media is strongest in the middle, owning rights and producing content, while the station next to the audience is held by Google, Meta, Netflix and Amazon. The rival stands between Indian content owners and their customers.

That is good or bad depending on the door. For a music label, the global platforms are customers who pay royalties. For a broadcaster, they are competitors for the same viewer and the same advertiser.

Use it when reading news. A cricket rights auction is an event at station one that sets costs at station two. A streaming app renegotiating music rates is an event at station four landing on the labels at station two. A shift in ad budgets to Instagram is a flow from station five that bypasses the Indian listed names entirely.

c3.story:
Who actually pays for Indian media? Mostly, not you. Advertisers are still the single biggest pay cheque, and that is both the industry's strength and its problem.

Take FMCG companies, the soap, shampoo and biscuit makers. They have long been the backbone of TV advertising. When rural demand is strong and raw materials are cheap, they launch products and spend on ads. When margins tighten, ad budgets are the first thing cut. So a weak FMCG quarter is a weak TV quarter, usually one step later.

Then the new advertisers: e-commerce, fintech and app companies, which bought heavily into digital ads and sports sponsorship when venture money flowed. Their spending follows funding cycles, and occasionally the law. When Parliament passed the online gaming law in August 2025 and banned real-money gaming, the fantasy-sports app that was then the Indian cricket team's jersey sponsor exited the deal. A whole category of big-spending sports advertisers vanished in weeks.

Auto, real estate and retail advertisers lean on print, outdoor and regional TV, and follow the festive season and local economies. That is why Dainik Bhaskar's ad pages fatten around Navratri and Diwali.

Not all money is advertising. Pay-TV households pay for channel packs, but their number has been shrinking since TRAI's 2019 tariff order, as viewers moved to free DTH and cheap streaming. Streaming platforms pay music labels and film owners for licences. Cinema-goers buy tickets and expensive popcorn. Brands and event organisers pay for songs in ads, reels and concerts. Foreign studios pay Prime Focus for visual effects, which means a Hollywood strike, like the one in 2023, lands in Mumbai.

Ad money is moving to platforms Indian companies do not own. The winners get paid by those platforms rather than compete with them.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read each in three lines: who pays, what they buy, what moves them.

  • The name identifies the payer: FMCG advertisers; e-commerce, fintech and app advertisers; auto, real estate and retail advertisers; pay-TV households; streaming platforms; cinema-goers; brands and event organisers; foreign studios and publishers.
  • The middle line is what they buy, which maps each tile to a door. The three advertiser tiles feed broadcasters and print. Pay-TV households feed broadcasters. Streaming platforms and brands feed the rights owners. Cinema-goers feed theatres. Foreign studios feed content services.
  • The last line is the driver to watch: rural demand, venture funding and regulatory bans, festive seasons, TRAI rules, platform subscriber growth, the film slate, short-video growth, Hollywood budgets.

Now count. Three of the eight tiles are advertisers, which tells you how much of this industry is still an advertising business. Then notice the split in fortunes: the advertiser and pay-TV tiles are the ones under pressure, while streaming platforms, cinema-goers and brands using songs are the growing ones.

The so-what makes the point sharply: the winners are those paid by the platforms rather than those competing with them. A music label's biggest customers are on the streaming-platforms and brands tiles. A broadcaster's are on the advertiser and pay-TV tiles. That alone explains most of the gap between their stocks.

c4.story:
Strip a media company down and the big cost is the same everywhere: content. What differs is how the content cost behaves over time, and that one difference separates a great business from a treadmill.

Follow a hundred rupees of a broadcaster's revenue. Nearly half goes on content: programming, rights, the serial, the reality show, the cricket. Another quarter goes to people, marketing and distribution. Depreciation is small. What is left is about a quarter. Not bad, until you notice the catch: next year, the broadcaster must spend that content money again, because yesterday's serial does not attract tomorrow's advertiser.

Now a music label. Under a third goes on content, mostly royalties to artists and the cost of new music. Another share, slightly under a third, goes to people and marketing. Depreciation is tiny. What is left is a bit over a third, and here is the beautiful part: the old catalogue does not need rebuying. A song recorded in the 1970s earns from a reel today, at almost no cost.

A music label is a landlord collecting rent on a building put up decades ago. A broadcaster redecorates every room every year.

Accounting makes this subtler. Broadcasters expense content as shows air, and they carry years of unaired shows and films as inventory, which can quietly pile up. A growing content inventory alongside slow ad receivables is a warning sign worth checking every year.

Multiplexes are a third species. Their content is film hire, a share of ticket revenue paid to the film's distributor. Their real fixed cost is the mall rent, which under lease accounting sits partly below EBITDA, so headline margins can flatter. A multiplex is a restaurant whose menu is written by someone else: the food and the rent are yours, the hits are not.

The investor's rule: separate the cost of content from the revenue it earns over time. Pay once and earn forever deserves a higher multiple than pay every year to stand still.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: broadcasters and streamers on one side, music and film rights owners on the other. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is content cost: programming, rights, royalties, film hire. For broadcasters it takes nearly half. For rights owners it takes under a third.
  • The opex bar is people, marketing, distribution and rent: about a quarter for broadcasters, a little more for rights owners, who spend on marketing and digital teams.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small on both.
  • The last bar is what is left: about a quarter for broadcasters, a bit over a third for rights owners.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for amounts.

The charts understate the real gap, because they show one year. The broadcaster's content bar comes back every year; much of the rights owner's catalogue does not.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Content cost and amortisation, advertising revenue, subscription and licensing revenue, working capital and content inventory, and lease rentals all get a yes. Depreciation, capex and interest are marked sometimes: small for labels and channels, heavy for multiplexes and parks.

The so-what is the practical test: for each company, ask how many years of revenue each rupee of content earns.

c5.story:
Media does not have one clock. It has a cyclical clock, advertising and the film slate, sitting on top of a structural escalator running downward for TV and print and upward for digital content owners.

The cycle started with a regulatory jolt. In 2019, TRAI's new tariff order forced channels to be priced individually. Viewers dropped channels they never watched, and pay-TV homes started shrinking. At the same time, cheap mobile data put video on every phone.

Then Covid shut cinemas for most of 2020, and ad spend collapsed. Streaming apps gained hundreds of millions of viewers stuck at home.

The boom of 2021 and 2022 was a spending spree. Ads came back. Streaming apps outbid each other for shows. And in 2022 the IPL media rights auction set a record, split between Disney Star for TV and Reliance's Viacom venture for digital. PVR and INOX announced their merger. Music labels signed richer streaming deals.

Then the bill arrived. From 2023, streaming platforms cut budgets and chased profit. JioCinema streamed the IPL free, upending the economics of paid cricket. The Zee-Sony merger collapsed in early 2024. Reliance and Disney merged into a single giant controlling much of TV viewing and cricket. Pay-TV homes kept shrinking and TV advertising stagnated.

In 2025, JioHotstar launched with cricket behind a low paywall, the online gaming law removed a big sports advertiser, and blockbusters like Chhaava and Saiyaara pulled audiences back into cinemas.

This is a bottom for some doors and a slow decline for others. Pick the door, not the sector.

Today the industry is split. Music labels report strong quarters; the explainer notes Tips grew revenue by around a third in Q2. TV ad revenue drifts lower and broadcasters cut costs. Multiplexes ride a healthier slate. Fewer bidders after consolidation also mean cheaper content for whoever still buys it.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, clockwise from the top: boom across 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust from 2023 to 2025, bottom across 2025 and 2026. The arrow sits at the bottom arc, labelled bottom, split by door, with the detail: TV shrinking, music and cinema rising. That label is unusual and important: the arrow is an average of doors moving in opposite directions. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: neutral for the tariff order, bust in 2020, boom for 2021 and 2022, bust again for 2023 and 2024, neutral in 2025, and the latest entry marked now, describing the split.

The four hands let you track each door separately.

  • TV advertising growth: flat to falling, arrow down. This is the broadcasters' hand. A return to growth would re-rate them.
  • Music streaming deal renewals: rising rates, arrow up. The labels' engine.
  • Multiplex footfalls and ticket prices: recovering, arrow up. The theatres' hand.
  • Content prices for sports and shows: falling, arrow up. Cheaper content helps whoever still buys it.

Three hands point up, one down, and the down one belongs to the biggest revenue pool, TV advertising. That is why the so-what refuses to call the sector as a whole: rights owners and cinemas are in an up-cycle, linear TV and print are not.

c6.story:
Three dials decide most of this industry's fortunes, and each one belongs to a different door.

The first is ad spending by FMCG and consumer brands. It is the biggest source of broadcast and print revenue. When Hindustan Unilever and its peers see rural volumes recover, they launch products and spend on TV. When raw materials spike and margins tighten, ad budgets get trimmed first. For a broadcaster, this dial is practically the whole story.

The second is paid streaming subscribers. Streaming services pay music royalties out of a pool that grows with paying users. Free, ad-supported listening pays far less per stream than a paid subscription. So as Indians move from free tiers to paid plans on Spotify, YouTube Music and the rest, the royalty pool grows, and it flows to labels. This dial decides the music door.

The third is film slate quality. It decides footfalls, ticket prices, food sales and music sales for the films' soundtracks. A quarter with two blockbusters can look like a different company from a quarter with none. This dial decides the theatres.

Below those sits one two-dot dial: rural consumption, which supports regional broadcasters like Sun TV and Hindi heartland print like Dainik Bhaskar through both ads and pay-TV renewals.

The one-dot dials are smaller nudges. Consumer inflation squeezes household budgets for tickets and subscriptions. Newsprint prices are print's biggest raw material. Interest rates matter for debt-funded screens and parks, and for start-up ad budgets. A weaker rupee helps services exporters like Prime Focus and MPS. And media index sentiment lifts or sinks the whole basket together, regardless of door.

Track FMCG ad spend for the broadcasters and paid subscribers for the labels. They rarely move together.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. This column tells you which door a dial belongs to. FMCG ad spend and rural consumption reach broadcasters and print. Paid streaming subscribers reach rights owners. Film slate quality reaches theatres and music. The rupee reaches services exporters.
  • A rise does: green up helps, red down hurts. Most rows here are green. Consumer inflation, newsprint and interest rates are the red ones.
  • Weight: one to three dots. This table has three three-dot rows, one per major door.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a matching series: the Nifty FMCG index as a stand-in for ad budgets, non-durables industrial output for rural consumption, recreation CPI, the money-market rate, the rupee and the Nifty Media index. Paid streaming subscribers, film slate quality and newsprint show a dash; you follow those through company commentary and the release calendar.

Read the three three-dot rows first, and read them separately. Do not average them. A strong film slate and rising streaming subscribers can coexist with falling FMCG ad spend, which is roughly the situation today, and it means the music and multiplex names are moving while broadcasters are not.

The so-what beneath the table compresses this: FMCG ad spending decides broadcasters, paid subscribers decide labels.

c7.story:
Indian media's bottlenecks fall into two groups: the ones that set a ceiling on TV and print, and the ones that make individual stocks dangerous.

The first ceiling is global platforms taking digital ads. Google and Meta capture most of India's digital advertising money. As ad budgets move from TV and print to digital, the money does not move from one Indian listed company to another. It moves out of Indian listed hands entirely. That is structural.

The second ceiling is cheap pay-TV and free DTH. TRAI price caps keep Indian pay-TV among the cheapest anywhere, and DD Free Dish plus cheap streaming drain paying homes. A broadcaster cannot raise prices to offset falling ads; the regulator caps them.

Then a two-sided bottleneck: Reliance-Disney dominance. Since the merger completed in late 2024, one group controls much of TV viewing and cricket rights. That gives it pricing power over advertisers and bargaining power over everyone else. For competing broadcasters, it is a headwind. For those selling to it, say a music label licensing songs, it is a big customer with a lot of leverage.

The recurring bottlenecks hit quarters. Cinema is hit-driven: a few films earn most of the box office, so a quarter with a weak slate looks terrible regardless of how well PVR INOX runs its screens. The theatre window, the gap before a film reaches streaming, keeps being renegotiated, and the shorter it is, the more viewers wait.

And then the bottleneck that matters most at the stock level: governance at promoter firms. Several listed media names have faced fund-diversion probes and SEBI orders. SEBI's 2023 order against Zee's promoters over alleged diversion of funds, which came months before the Sony merger collapsed, is the best-known example. Governance discounts in this sector are large and persistent.

In media, the biggest single stock risk is not the audience. It is the promoter.

Piracy is the slow one: pirated cricket and films still eat revenue despite court orders.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. Use the label to decide how to treat it.

  • Structural: global platforms taking digital ads, and cheap pay-TV with free DTH. Permanent ceilings on TV and print. They belong in your valuation of any broadcaster: do not pay for a recovery these rows forbid.
  • Two-sided: Reliance-Disney dominance. Bad for rival broadcasters, mixed for suppliers who sell content to it.
  • Recurring: hit-driven cinema, the shrinking theatre window, and governance at promoter firms. The first two move multiplex quarters. The third moves individual stocks, sometimes violently, when a regulator's order lands.
  • Slow: piracy, a persistent leak that court orders chip at.

Read the so-what as the priority order: the first two rows set the ceiling for TV and print, and the governance row is the single biggest stock-level risk in the sector.

Now map the rows to doors. Broadcasters face almost every row. Theatres face the hit-driven and window rows. Music labels face few of them; the platforms taking digital ads are, for a label, customers. That is the bottleneck table's version of the call.

Practical use: for any media name you hold, check the governance row first. Read the promoter's related-party transactions and any pending SEBI matters before you read the ad growth.

c8.story:
Media's rulebook has an unusual property: a single regulatory decision can rewrite a business model overnight, and it has happened several times in this cycle.

The clearest case was TRAI's 2019 tariff order. By forcing channels to be priced individually and capping bouquet prices, it ended the era of broadcasters quietly bundling weak channels with strong ones. Viewers dropped the channels they never watched, and pay-TV homes started shrinking. TRAI's caps are still live, which is why broadcasters cannot simply raise subscription prices to offset falling ads.

The newest case is the online gaming law of 2025. By banning real-money gaming, it removed one of the biggest sports and digital advertisers from the market almost overnight; the fantasy-sports app on the Indian team's jersey gave up the sponsorship within days. For anyone selling cricket ad inventory, a whole category of buyer vanished.

The Copyright Act and royalty rules are the legal foundation of a music label. They define who owns a song and how royalties are paid, and court rulings on licensing rates can move a label's value. The Competition Commission approved the Reliance-Disney merger with conditions and keeps watching ad and rights bundling. SEBI enforces disclosure and investigates fund diversion; its orders against promoters have hit several media stocks hard.

CBFC certification can move a film's release date, and with it a multiplex's quarter. The IT Rules for digital media give streaming platforms a code of ethics and a grievance system, and complaints can force edits.

For a broadcaster, TRAI sets the price. For a label, the Copyright Act is the moat.

The one to watch is the draft Broadcasting Services Bill from the information and broadcasting ministry, which could bring streaming under content and licensing rules similar to TV. That would change the playing field between channels and apps.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Always: CBFC certification, the Copyright Act and royalty rules, the Competition Commission and SEBI. Permanent fixtures. For music labels, the copyright row is the most important line in the table. For investors in promoter-run firms, the SEBI row is.
  • Live: TRAI's tariff order for broadcasting, and the IT Rules for digital media. TRAI's caps limit how much broadcasters can raise subscription fees, which keeps them dependent on advertising.
  • New: the Online Gaming Act, 2025. It already happened, and its effect, a big advertiser category removed, shows up in sports and digital ad revenue.
  • Coming: the information and broadcasting ministry's draft Broadcasting Services Bill, which could bring streaming under rules similar to TV.

Now map rows to doors. Broadcasters face TRAI, the Competition Commission, the gaming ban's ad hit and the coming bill: the most crowded rulebook. Music labels mainly face the copyright row, which protects them. Theatres face CBFC. Promoter-run companies of any door face SEBI.

The pattern mirrors the call: the door with the thinnest rulebook exposure and the strongest legal moat is the one the call prefers.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks who keeps the money once it comes in. Run Indian media through it and you get one of the starkest contrasts anywhere on these pages.

Start with broadcasters. Rivalry is fierce: they fight a dominant Reliance-Disney combine and global apps for every viewer and every ad rupee. Suppliers have the upper hand: stars, producers and above all cricket boards charge top prices, and the IPL auction is a lesson in supplier power. Buyers, the advertisers, can move budgets to Google and Meta overnight. Entrants are everywhere, because any creator can start a channel on YouTube for free. And substitutes are the deepest threat of all: short video, gaming and social media take viewing time from TV every year.

Now run a music label through the same test. Rivalry is low, because each song is unique; nobody substitutes one iconic Lata Mangeshkar track for another label's song. Suppliers have little leverage, since labels already own their catalogues. Buyers, the streaming apps, need the hit songs and must license them. Entrants cannot rebuild a decades-old catalogue at any price.

And here is the twist: on substitutes, the very force that crushes TV helps music. Short video is a substitute for TV viewing, but every reel needs a song. When TikTok was banned in 2020 and Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts filled the gap, music labels gained new licensing customers.

Short video is the broadcaster's substitute and the music label's customer.

That is why rights owners keep the profit: everyone else, from apps to reels to brands, needs their content. Broadcasters and print fight harder each year to keep what they earn.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: broadcasters and streamers, and music and film rights owners. Look at overall size first. The broadcaster shape is large, reaching the outer ring on two spokes. The rights-owner shape is small and compact, hugging the centre.

  • Rivalry: broadcasters at the outer ring, rights owners well inside.
  • Supplier: broadcasters reach far out, because stars and cricket boards set prices. Rights owners sit near the centre.
  • Buyer: broadcasters reach far, as advertisers can move to Google and Meta. Rights owners stay modest.
  • Entrants: broadcasters in the middle, as YouTube creators keep arriving; rights owners near the centre.
  • Substitutes: broadcasters at the outer ring again; rights owners modest. This is the spoke with the widest gap in meaning, as the story explains: the same short-video trend hurts one and helps the other.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason.

Theatres and print are not drawn, but you can place them. A multiplex chain would score high on supplier, because producers control the films, and moderate on substitutes, given streaming. Print would look much like the broadcaster shape.

c10.story:
Media results can be confusing because the four doors report such different things. A broadcaster talks about viewership share, a label about streaming deals, a multiplex about footfalls. Eight numbers cover all of them.

Ad revenue growth comes first: does the medium still attract advertisers? For TV, simply being positive is the bar right now. Digital arms should grow much faster.

Subscription or licensing revenue share tells you how much of the revenue is steady rather than cyclical. A broadcaster with rising subscription share is becoming less hostage to FMCG budgets. A label is mostly licensing already, which is part of why its earnings are smoother.

EBITDA margin is content cost discipline, with very different norms by door. Content cost as a share of revenue is the key question for broadcasters: is spending buying growth, or just holding ground? If content cost rises while revenue stalls, the broadcaster is running to stand still.

Inventory and receivable days catch two quiet problems: unaired content piling up on the balance sheet, and advertisers paying late. Both have been warning signs at stressed broadcasters.

For multiplexes, the engine is footfalls, average ticket price and spend per head on food and drinks. Food is the high-margin part: the popcorn earns more than the ticket.

Then net debt to EBITDA: can a theatre chain or park survive a weak slate? Labels and broadcasters should hold net cash. And ROCE, which tells you whether content spending earns its keep. For a music label with a paid-off catalogue, it can be very high.

For a broadcaster, watch content cost. For a multiplex, watch the popcorn.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question for each company. Map each row to a door: ad growth, subscription share and content cost for broadcasters; footfalls, ticket price and spend per head for multiplexes; ROCE and EBITDA margin for everyone, with very different norms.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, as rules of thumb. Several rows split by door. EBITDA margin has separate bars for broadcasters, music labels and multiplexes, with labels expected to run highest. Net debt has one bar for multiplexes and expects net cash for labels and broadcasters. ROCE expects much more from labels than from broadcasters.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of listed media companies. Most rows have one; subscription share and the multiplex footfall row come from company presentations and show a dash.

A strong caution here: the median blends a declining broadcaster, a fast-growing label, a theatre chain, a newspaper, a visual-effects house and an education publisher. In a split industry, the median describes almost no actual company. Compare each name with its own door's good mark first.

The best routine: for broadcasters, put ad growth beside content cost share each quarter; for labels, licensing growth and ROCE; for multiplexes, footfalls and net debt.

c11.story:
Media gives early warnings that are easy to read if you know which door each belongs to.

Some arrive in the same quarter. Festive timing matters enormously: Diwali and Durga Puja carry the year's biggest ad spend, so whether a festival falls in one quarter or the next can swing reported growth. Regulatory bans on ad categories land the quarter they happen, as the gaming ban showed in 2025.

Most signals speak one quarter ahead. FMCG companies set ad budgets a quarter before the ads air, so their volume growth and ad-spend commentary is the broadcaster's next quarter. The film release calendar tells you about footfalls and soundtrack sales next quarter. The cricket calendar and rights deals matter twice over: an IPL season or an India tour lifts ads for the rights holder and drains them from everyone else. Newsprint and paper import prices show up in print margins a quarter later.

The furthest dot is streaming paid-subscriber growth, two quarters out. Royalty pools grow with paying subscribers, and then flow to labels through renewals.

Combine the three big signals and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when brand ad spending is growing, paid streaming subscribers are rising and the film slate is filling theatres. But this rule comes with an unusual twist: two of three means a recovery for the doors those signs belong to, and one of three means a door-specific story.

Today two of three are ticking: streaming subscribers and theatres. The missing one, brand ad spending, is the broadcasters' sign.

Own the rights, rent the screens, avoid the shrinking pipes.

That is the call in one line. Music labels and the multiplex chain are where the ticks are; linear broadcasters and print are where the cross is.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read its channel.

  • Same quarter, far left: festive season timing and regulatory bans on ad categories. These explain the quarter you are in.
  • One quarter ahead: FMCG volume growth and ad-spend commentary, the film release calendar, the cricket calendar and rights deals, and newsprint prices.
